scenarios.name: Setup market and prices
Setup players: 1 camel, score 0
Deck starts with 20 cards
Round 2 is led by seat 2
Round 4 is led by seat 1
Round 10 restocks one cloth
Round 3 restocks one silver
Round 5 restocks one camel
Round 7 restocks one diamond
One draw per round shrinks the deck by 1
Draw into a full hand is discarded
Draw into a non-full hand is kept, nothing discarded
Private draw leaves the public market untouched
TAKE Silver 3 pays 2 camels into the market
TAKE beyond camels+1 or beyond hand limit is not offered
CAMELS takes all market camels; not offered when none left
Selling 1 diamond/silver or more than held is not offered
Selling a single cloth is legal
Selling 2 silver scores 2 x 5
Selling 3 silver adds +3
Selling 4 cloth adds +5 and the price floors at 1
Selling 5 diamond adds +8
Selling 2 diamond at 7 scores 14, price becomes 5
Price floor: 2 cloth sold at price 2 leaves price 1
Illegal sale is not offered and the other seat's state is unchanged
Each turn's public result is visible after the round
Camel majority earns +5 at the end
Tied camels give no bonus
Cards left in hand score nothing
Equal final scores share the win

spec_choices.why: The designer fixed 2. The turn-order schedule, the camel majority and the market race are all built for two rivals, so a third seat would break the schedule.

spec_choices.what: Seat 1 is player A and seat 2 is player B
spec_choices.why: The source names A and B. Mapping them to seats lets the turn-order schedule be applied.

spec_choices.what: Only legal actions are offered, with PASS offered only when nothing is legal
spec_choices.why: The platform asks that a seat is never offered what it may not do. The source's illegal-is-a-pass rule is kept as a fallback for missing answers.
The source has no talk. It is a pure two-player race, and talk would add words without changing incentives.

spec_choices.what: The camel bonus is applied in an update step that runs only when round == 16, just before the ending check
spec_choices.why: This places the 'after round 16' bonus in a single step with a condition.

A thoughtful player times sales before prices fall, uses private draws to plan set bonuses, takes camels to win the +5 majority or to fund multi-card takes, and denies the opponent restocked goods using the public schedule.

simplifications.what: The deck is a hidden table list, and the 'top card' is drawn at random from it
simplifications.why: Drawing at random from a shuffled list is equivalent to taking the top card of a deck shuffled once.

simplifications.what: Turn order is implemented as two ask steps addressed to first_seat and then to the other seat
simplifications.why: The engine's step list is fixed. The acting seat is chosen from the table attribute first_seat.

variation.original_summary: Jaipur is a two-player card-trading game. Players take goods or camels from a shared five-card market and sell sets of one good for falling-price tokens, with bonuses for large sets and for owning the most camels; the best of three rounds wins. The previous XColos variation turned it into a 16-round, three-good, count-based duel with a public restock schedule and a private draw each round.

review.evidence: No thoughtless policy wins. Always CAMELS scores at most 5 and loses to one Diamond pair sale (14). Always SELL mostly passes or dumps singletons. Always TAKE never scores. Always pass scores 0. Sell-early (locking a high price) versus hold (set bonuses) is a real tension. The previous variation still gave the seats unequal value. A had first refusal on both sellable market Diamonds (rounds 5 and 11), and B's only Diamond, in round 16, could never be sold. Cloth first refusals ran 3 to B and 2 to A. A also acted last in round 16 with full information. The net edge to A was about 8 to 12 points, comparable to the margin between equal players.

Points come from timing sales against a falling price ladder (Diamond pairs 14, 10, 6), building 3+ sets for +3/+5/+8, choosing when to spend camels on multi-card takes, and denying the opponent market cards. A careful player reliably beats a random or greedy one. Private draws add variance, but every one of them is offset by public market play.

A weak player can still make a few pair sales. A strong player can keep improving: tracking the opponent's likely hand from the public deck composition and their takes and sales, preempting their sale by selling first to crash the price, and managing the camel race near the end.

Hands and private draws are hidden. The deck composition and every take and sale are public, so a player can infer the opponent's hand. The restock schedule is public, so planning over several rounds pays.
Scores are price times count plus fixed bonuses plus a camel bonus. Everything is arithmetic on tracked counts.
Turn-based, text-only, with no board. It uses count attributes and one deck draw per round, takes 16 rounds, and stays within the step limits.

problems: P1: The Diamond restock schedule gave player A first refusal on both sellable market Diamonds, while B's only Diamond came in round 16, when it was unsellable. This was a swing of about 10 to 14 points.
P2: Cloth first refusals were uneven: B 3, A 2.
P3: A strict odd/even alternation made A act last in round 16 with full knowledge, and restocks were not paired by seat, so per-type first refusals could not be balanced.
P4: Goods restocked in the last round can only be taken, never sold, so whoever gets first refusal on a last-round goods card gains nothing, while the other seat may have lost a real card earlier.

changes.what: Turn order follows the ABBA pattern: A, B, B, A, A, B, B, A, A, B, B, A, A, B, B, A. Each player is first in 8 rounds. A makes the game's first action; B makes the game's last action.
changes.why: Pairs the rounds so that each consecutive pair (1-2, 3-4, ...) has one A-first round and one B-first round. It also splits the first-move and last-move advantages between the seats instead of giving A both opening tempo and final-information play.

changes.what: The restock schedule repeats the same type in both rounds of each pair. Cloth goes in rounds 1-2 and 9-10, Silver in 3-4 and 11-12, Camel in 5-6 and 15-16, and Diamond in 7-8 and 13-14.
changes.why: Each seat gets first refusal on exactly 2 Diamonds, 2 Silver, 2 Cloth and 2 Camels. The Diamonds arrive at comparable times for both players: B first in round 7 and A first in round 8; A first in round 13 and B first in round 14. All of them come early enough to be sold.

changes.what: The same pairing gives each seat exactly 2 Cloth first refusals.
The final pair, rounds 15 and 16, restocks Camels instead of goods.
changes.why: A card taken in round 16 can still matter, through the camel majority. No unsellable goods card is ever restocked.

keeps: The take-or-sell turn with a hand limit of 7
Taking all camels from the market
A falling price ladder per good, with bonuses for sets of 3, 4 and 5 or more
A minimum sale of 2 for the precious goods
Hidden hands and private draws from a deck of public composition

recommendation.reason: The core tension of selling early to lock a price versus holding for set bonuses, and the hidden-hand inference, work well. Only the seat asymmetry needed fixing, which a paired schedule and an ABBA turn order solve.

variation.name: Jaipur Bazaar (Balanced Schedule)
variation.summary: A two-player, 16-round duel of taking goods from a shared market and selling sets on falling prices. Hands are hidden, and the restock schedule is public and paired so that both seats get equal first refusals.
variation.rules:
CARDS AND STATE
- There are three goods types (Diamond, Silver, Cloth) and camels.
- Each player has a hidden hand, recorded as counts of Diamond, Silver and Cloth. Each player also has a public camel herd (a count) and a public score.
- The market is public and holds counts of Diamond, Silver, Cloth and Camel.
- Each good has a public price. The starting prices are Diamond 7, Silver 5, Cloth 3.
- A private deck of 20 goods cards is shuffled once at the start: 5 Diamond, 7 Silver, 8 Cloth. The composition is public.

SETUP
- The market starts with 2 Camel, 1 Silver and 1 Cloth.
- Each player starts with 1 Silver and 1 Cloth in hand, 1 camel in herd, and score 0.

TURN ORDER
- The round's first player is:
  - A in rounds 1, 4, 5, 8, 9, 12, 13 and 16;
  - B in rounds 2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 11, 14 and 15.
- The other player is second in that round.

EACH ROUND (16 rounds)
1. Restock: add one card to the market according to this public schedule.
   - Rounds 1 and 2: Cloth. Rounds 3 and 4: Silver. Rounds 5 and 6: Camel. Rounds 7 and 8: Diamond.
   - Rounds 9 and 10: Cloth. Rounds 11 and 12: Silver. Rounds 13 and 14: Diamond. Rounds 15 and 16: Camel.
2. Private draw: the round's first player draws the top deck card into their hand.
   - Only they see its type. Both players are told that a draw happened.
   - If that hand already holds 7 goods, the drawn card is discarded instead, and only the drawer learns its type.
3. The first player takes one turn, which is announced publicly.
4. The second player takes one turn, which is announced publicly.

A TURN: choose exactly one action.
- TAKE <good> <n>: take n cards (n at least 1) of one goods type from the market into your hand. Three conditions apply:
  - the market must hold at least n of that type;
  - you must return n-1 camels from your herd to the market, so you must own at least n-1 camels;
  - your hand must hold at most 7 goods afterwards.
- CAMELS: move all camels in the market into your herd. The market must hold at least 1 camel.
- SELL <good> <n>: discard n cards of one good from your hand.
  - Diamond and Silver need n of at least 2. Cloth needs n of at least 1.
  - You score n times that good's current price.
  - You also score a bonus: +3 if n is 3, +5 if n is 4, +8 if n is 5 or more.
  - Then that good's price drops by n, to a minimum of 1.
- An illegal or missing choice counts as a pass: nothing happens.
- What is announced publicly: the action type, the good and n. The type of a privately drawn card is never announced.

END
- After round 16, the player with strictly more camels in their herd scores +5. If camels are tied, nobody gets the bonus.
- Cards left in hand score nothing.
variation.objective: After the camel bonus, the player with the higher score wins. Equal scores are a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Each seat now has first refusal on 2 sellable Diamonds, 2 Silver, 2 Cloth and 2 Camels, and each draws privately 8 times. The first-move edge (A) and the last-move edge (B) offset each other, so seat results should be close to even. Simple policies still lose: always CAMELS scores at most 5, always pass scores 0, and always SELL dumps singletons at falling prices. Play centres on reading the opponent's hidden hand from the public deck composition and their takes, racing to sell before they crash a price, deciding when 3+ sets are worth the wait, and contesting the final camel restocks for the +5 bonus. The private draws add some variance, but contested market cards and price preemption let a better player overcome a worse deal. There is no talk phase, because with two players and a zero-sum winner rule talk would add nothing to reason about.

balanced.evidence: Thoughtless policies, judged by the winner rule. (1) Always CAMELS. Camels in the system: 1 per herd, 2 in the market, and restocks in rounds 2, 6, 9 and 13, so at most about 6 camels reach this player. When the market has no camel the action is illegal and counts as a pass. This player earns no goods and scores only the +5 camel bonus. A sensible opponent who makes one Diamond pair sale (2x7=14) already beats it, so it loses almost every game, including to random play, which sometimes completes a sale. (2) Always SELL the first or largest legal set. It is mostly illegal, so mostly passes, and it dumps singletons early. It loses to anyone who builds sets: 5 Diamonds sold at once score 35+8=43, while pairs score 14+10+6. (3) Always TAKE the first option. It fills the hand and never scores, so it loses. (4) Always pass. Score 0, loses. No option is strictly dominant. Selling early locks in a high price, because each sale drops the price by n permanently, while holding builds set bonuses (+3/+5/+8). This is a real preemption tension. Price ladder for Diamond pair sales: 14, then price 5; 10, then price 3; 6, then price 1. A 3-set at 7 scores 21+3=24 and leaves price 4. SEAT EDGE, which is the failure. The round's first player has first refusal on the restocked card and can take a single card for free (TAKE n=1 costs 0 camels). Diamond restocks fall in rounds 5 (A first), 11 (A first) and 16 (B first). A Diamond taken in round 16 can never be sold, because you cannot take and sell in the same turn, so B's only first refusal on a Diamond is worthless. A therefore has uncontested first refusal on both usable market Diamonds. Each is worth about 5 to 7 points to A and denies B the same, a swing of about 10 to 14 points. Other restocks: Silver in rounds 3, 8, 12, 15 goes A, B, B, A (even). Cloth in rounds 1, 4, 7, 10, 14 goes A, B, A, B, B (B +1, worth about 3). Camel in rounds 2, 6, 9, 13 goes B, B, A, A (even). A also acts last in round 16 with full knowledge of B's final move. Net structural edge to A: roughly 8 to 12 points, which is comparable to the margin between equally skilled players. Both players can win, but the seats are not symmetric.

playable.evidence: The state is fully specified. It has 3 hand counts per player, herds, scores, 4 market counts and 3 prices, about 17 to 19 attributes, which is within the limit of 20. Deck: 20 cards with 16 draws, so it never runs out. Hidden elements: the private hands and deck order, which is within 3. Random draws: 1 per round. Choice steps: 2 sequential turns per round, within the limit of 4. Rounds: 16, within 40. The 17 stated steps are within 20. Legality conditions are arithmetic: market count at least n, camels at least n-1, and hand at most 7 after a take. Illegal choices become a pass. Sell order is clear: score n times the price plus the bonus, then the price drops, with a floor of 1. The hand-limit discard is defined. The winner is decided by arithmetic on the scores the game keeps, including the camel tie rule. No board, clock, judge, trading or binding promises are needed. With two players, talk is unnecessary. The game is not a repeated cooperation dilemma, so the late-round betrayal check does not apply. Sequential turns are correct here because the order matters.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: Chance enters only through the 16 private draws, 8 per player, which supply roughly half of each player's goods. Diamond split example: if 4 of the 16 drawn cards are Diamonds, P(2-2)=6*924/12870=0.43, P(1-3 or 3-1)=0.49 and P(0-4 or 4-0)=0.08. So in about 57% of games one player draws at least 2 more Diamonds, worth about 10 to 14 points. That luck is real, but skill levers are larger. (a) Sale timing against the permanent price drop: a 5-set of Diamonds scores 43, against 30 from pairs. (b) Preempting: selling a pair to crash the price before an opponent you infer is building a set. (c) Market take and denial decisions. (d) Camel management for the +5 bonus and to afford multi-card takes. (e) Inference: the opponent's hand is exactly known except for their draws. Deck composition is public, and their take and sell pattern reveals what they hold, which you can act on through preemptive sales and denial. A reasoning player is clearly favoured over a naive one, and the draw luck is of a size that good play can overcome. Once the seat edge is removed, mirror play leaves draws as a tiebreak-scale factor, not the sole decider.

required_changes: Remove the first-player edge on the market Diamonds. Move the Diamond restocks so each seat has first refusal on the same number of sellable Diamonds, for example Diamonds in rounds 5 (A first) and 10 (B first), with round 16 restocking a Camel or Cloth instead. Alternatively, stop restocking a Diamond in the final round, where it is unsellable, and give the 16th card to a round where B is first.
Even the Cloth first-refusal count (currently B 3 vs A 2), for example by swapping the round 14 Cloth with the round 13 Camel.

Optionally offset A's last-action advantage in round 16 by making the final round's turn order the reverse of the round-1 order, or by adding a small compensating bonus for B. Then recheck that each seat's first-refusal value is equal.

balanced.evidence:
SUPPLY. Both hands start with 1S+1C. The market starts with 1S+1C+2 camels. The schedule adds Cloth 4, Silver 4, Diamond 4 and Camel 4. Sixteen private draws come from the 20-card deck. Each player is first in exactly 8 rounds, so each makes exactly 8 draws.

SEAT ORDER. Rounds pair as A,B | B,A | A,B and so on, in an ABBA pattern. Every scheduled restock type is split evenly on first pick:
- Cloth: rounds 1(A), 2(B), 9(A), 10(B)
- Silver: rounds 3(B), 4(A), 11(B), 12(A)
- Camel: rounds 5(A), 6(B), 15(B), 16(A)
- Diamond: rounds 7(B), 8(A), 13(A), 14(B)
Remaining asymmetries:
- A acts first in round 1.
- B has the very last action in round 16.
- A gets first claim on the last camel restock (round 16), but B got round 15's.
The last move only lets B sell knowing A's final action. Selling after A cannot reduce A's score, so the edge is small and roughly offsets A's round-1 tempo.

PRICE AND BONUS TABLE. Each sale drops the price by n, to a minimum of 1.
- Diamond at 7: 2 cards = 14 (price to 5); 3 = 21+3 = 24 (to 4); 4 = 28+5 = 33 (to 3); 5 = 35+8 = 43 (to 2).
- Silver at 5: 2 = 10 (to 3); 3 = 15+3 = 18 (to 2); 4 = 20+5 = 25 (to 1).
- Cloth at 3: 1 = 3 (to 2); 3 = 9+3 = 12 (to 1); 5 = 15+8 = 23 (to 1).
At price 1, set bonuses dominate (5 Cloth at 1 = 13). This gives a real tension between selling early to catch the price and holding for a bonus while racing the opponent.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES UNDER THE WINNER RULE (higher score wins):
- Always pass: scores 0, so it loses to any player who makes one sale. Fail as a strategy.
- Always CAMELS: at most 6 of the 8 camels pass through the market, giving +5 at most. Any opponent who sells 2 Silver once (10) beats it, so it loses.
- Always sell the largest legal set immediately: it captures the 7/5 tops early but forfeits the +5/+8 bonuses. A patient player selling 4-5 Diamonds at 5 makes 25-33+ against 14+10. Each policy loses to a sensible counter, so it does not always win.
- Always TAKE 1 of the first legal good, never sell: scores 0 and loses.
- Random play: a sensible player beats it on both price timing and set bonuses.
No action is strictly better regardless of the opponent: the value of selling now depends on whether the opponent will hit the same good first. No policy never loses. Both seats can win.

playable.evidence:
The rules cover every situation:
- Legality of TAKE (supply, n-1 camels, hand ≤7), CAMELS (≥1 in market) and SELL (minimum n per type, sufficient cards).
- Illegal or missing actions count as a pass.
- A draw into a full hand is discarded.
- Price floor is 1. The bonus tiers are exact.
- Camel ties give nobody the bonus. Leftover cards score nothing.
- An equal score is a draw.
- What is public is specified: action type, good and n. Drawn types are never announced.

The game is finite (16 fixed rounds) and decided purely by arithmetic on tracked numbers.

Limits against the platform caps:
- Steps 14 ≤ 20.
- Choices: 2 per round. Because the first player alternates, this may need 4 when-conditioned choice steps, which is still ≤ 4.
- Attributes: 2×(3 hand + herd + score) + 4 market + 3 prices + deck + round ≈ 19 ≤ 20.
- Hidden elements: 2 hands, or 3 counting the deck, ≤ 3.
- One random draw per round, using the shared_deck_draw workaround.

The round-indexed restock and draw recipient are single-step `when`/`if` conditions, not conditional blocks. No board, judge, clock, trading or binding agreement is needed. Two players with no cooperative dilemma means talk is not needed and the repeated-cooperation concern does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
The only randomness is which 8 of the 20 deck cards each player draws. Diamonds drawn per player follow a hypergeometric distribution: mean 2, variance 0.947, covariance -0.632. The A-minus-B Diamond difference therefore has an SD of about 1.78 cards.

A Diamond is worth about 3 points more than an average good. That puts the luck swing at roughly 5-6 points SD, out of totals around 40-60 per player.

Skill levers are worth more than that:
- Being first to sell Diamonds at 7 rather than 5 gains +2 per card.
- Reaching 4-5 card sets earns +5/+8.
- The camel majority is worth +5.
- Contesting the 4 public Diamonds and the market flow, where only about 0.75 goods are added net per round, also pays.

There is a lot to infer. The opponent's hand is hidden, but you know they have exactly k draws, every public take and sell, and the deck composition (5D/7S/8C). That lets a player estimate the opponent's Diamond and Silver holdings and pre-empt or delay sales.

With equal good play the draws shift the edge but do not alone decide the winner: sale timing and set-versus-price choices still dominate. A stronger reasoner is clearly favoured.
